title: Tanning Misinformation Posted by Businesses on Social Media and Related Perceptions of Adolescent and Young Adult White Non-Hispanic Women: Mixed Methods Study (Moreno, Jenkins & Lazovich, JMIR Dermatology 2021)
screen_reason: Mixed-methods study with (a) a content analysis of 4,956 Facebook posts from 147 US indoor-tanning business pages coded against dermatological evidence, reporting the share of posts in each health-misinformation category (Vitamin D 73 posts = 1.5%; tanning as medical treatment 31 = 0.6%; base tan 29 = 0.5%), and (b) interviews with 46 young women, 43% (20/46) of whom reported having seen tanning-salon posts about Vitamin D. Both a CONTENT share of items with a denominator and a self-reported (RECALL) exposure share are present, so the paper is eligible.

estimates.measure_type: % of sampled tanning-business Facebook posts that promoted UV tanning as a safe way to get Vitamin D (the largest misinformation category)
estimates.value_raw: n=73, 1.5% (Abstract); the Results text states the same 73 posts as 1.3%; 73/4956 = 1.47%
estimates.denominator: 4,956 Facebook posts sampled from 147 indoor tanning business pages (3 most-followed qualifying pages per US state) over one year, sampling the final post of every third day
estimates.definition: Post coded into the 'About Vitamin D' misinformation category, i.e. describing indoor UV tanning as a safe/healthy way to get Vitamin D, which the authors judge misinformation against American Academy of Dermatology guidance (tanning beds emit mostly UVA and are not a safe route to adequate Vitamin D)
estimates.misinfo_def: For this study we define misinformation as inaccurate or false information.
estimates.source_quote: Among 9 health misinformation topics identified, the most common was the promotion of UV tanning as a safe way to get Vitamin D (n=73, 1.5%). An example post was “Stop by Body and Sol to get your daily dose of Vitamin D.”
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (Results) p. 1; Results, Social Media Content Analysis, p. 4; Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Trained coders applied an author-developed codebook built from prior codebooks, a literature review and pilot coding; each post was the unit of analysis; interrater agreement 84%-99% at the start and 91%-100% at the end of coding across the health misinformation variables. External standards cited are the American Academy of Dermatology and a US House of Representatives investigative report on false and misleading indoor-tanning claims.
estimates.moderator_quote: For each of the 50 states, we evaluated 3 tanning business profiles to capture range and variation across businesses. We used purposeful sampling to identify profiles ... From the list of search results, we reviewed the first 10 business profiles listed, and from those profiles, we selected the 3 business profiles that had the largest number of followers.
estimates.notes: The denominator is a systematic sample of posts (final post of every third day, duplicates skipped), not the full year of posting, and pages were chosen as the 3 most-followed per state, hence denom_selection=curated. Internal inconsistencies flagged for the adjudicator: the Abstract says 9 misinformation topics and gives 1.5% for the 73 Vitamin D posts, while the Results say 8 topics (Table 1 lists 8) and give 1.3% for the same 73 posts; 73/4956 = 1.47%, so 1.5% is the arithmetically correct figure and is used here. The Abstract also mislabels the 31 posts as 'promoting tanning for health benefits (0.62%)' whereas Table 1 shows 'About health benefits of tanning' has n=7 and 'Tanning as a medical treatment' has n=31.

estimates.measure_type: % of sampled tanning-business Facebook posts promoting indoor tanning as a medical treatment
estimates.denominator: 4,956 Facebook posts sampled from 147 indoor tanning business pages across 50 states over one year
estimates.definition: Post coded as claiming tanning is a treatment or preventive for illness (acne, eczema, seasonal depression, cancer, autism); the authors note there is no evidence for tanning as a safe treatment for mental illness, inflammatory disease, sleep problems or pain disorders
estimates.misinfo_def: For this study we define misinformation as inaccurate or false information.
estimates.source_quote: A second category was misinformation about tanning as a medical treatment (n=31 posts, 0.6%), for example,
estimates.page_loc: Results, Social Media Content Analysis, p. 4; Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same trained-coder codebook procedure; interrater agreement 84%-99% at start, 91%-100% at end
estimates.moderator_quote: Each social media post was considered the unit of analysis and was thus categorized and coded based on which constructs were represented in that post.
estimates.notes: One of eight misinformation categories in the same post sample; marked definition_variant because it is a narrower category within the same country x platform cell as the Vitamin D row. Categories are not mutually exclusive (a post is coded for every construct it represents), so category shares must not be summed. The example post that follows in the article is '...the flu is not a season, it’s an inability to adapt due to decreased sun exposure…' (set off as a block quote, hence not part of the contiguous span).

estimates.measure_type: % of sampled tanning-business Facebook posts promoting misinformation about the benefits of a 'base tan'
estimates.denominator: 4,956 Facebook posts sampled from 147 indoor tanning business pages across 50 states over one year
estimates.definition: Post coded as claiming a base tan prevents sunburn or protects before a vacation; the authors state there is no evidence a base tan protects against sunburn or cancer risk
estimates.misinfo_def: For this study we define misinformation as inaccurate or false information.
estimates.source_quote: Another category of misinformation was promoting misinformation about the benefits of a “base tan” (n=29 posts, 0.5%) The posts often argued that a base tan would prevent sunburn or was a protective measure to take prior to a vacation.
estimates.page_loc: Results, Social Media Content Analysis, p. 4; Table 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same trained-coder codebook procedure; interrater agreement 84%-99% at start, 91%-100% at end
estimates.moderator_quote: Trained coders reviewed 1 year of content on each business social media profile. ... our content analysis strategy was to evaluate 1 post per day, selected as the final post of that day, every third day of the month.
estimates.notes: This is the lower bound of the range the authors summarise in the Discussion: 'an overall low frequency of social media posts promoting health misinformation (range 0.5%-1.5%)'. Category shares are not mutually exclusive and no overall misinformation share is reported anywhere in the paper.

estimates.country: United States (26 states represented among interviewees)
estimates.measure_type: % of interviewed young women who reported having seen social media posts from tanning salons about Vitamin D (the study's main misinformation category)
estimates.value_raw: Approximately half (20/46, 43%) of participants reported seeing social media posts from tanning salons about Vitamin D
estimates.denominator: 46 White non-Hispanic women aged 16-23 (mean 20, SD 2) recruited by Facebook advertisement, all of whom had tanned indoors in the past year; 26 states represented
estimates.definition: Participant answered that they had seen indoor tanning businesses post on social media about Vitamin D, when asked directly after the interviewer described the content-analysis finding
estimates.misinfo_def: For this study we define misinformation as inaccurate or false information.
estimates.source_quote: As Vitamin D was the most common category of social media misinformation posts, we asked participants whether they had seen indoor tanning businesses post on social media about Vitamin D. Approximately half (20/46, 43%) of participants reported seeing social media posts from tanning salons about Vitamin D: I have [seen that] a few times... [Participant]
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported recall in a semi-structured phone interview; the interviewer first gave 'a brief overview of the study findings regarding observations of health misinformation on social media', so the recall question is prompted and cued by the researcher's own framing
estimates.moderator_quote: we recruited participants via Facebook advertisements. A Facebook advertisement was created and targeted to a national sample of women ages 16 through 23 years. ... Interested participants were directed to a website to complete eligibility screening to ensure they met inclusion criteria (experienced indoor tanning in the past year and were in our target demographic).
estimates.notes: BORDERLINE: (a) tiny purposive qualitative sample (n=46) of a deliberately at-risk group (White non-Hispanic women 16-23 who tanned indoors in the past year, recruited through Facebook ads), which the authors say was not intended to support external validity; (b) the question asks about seeing posts 'about Vitamin D' rather than about misinformation as such, though in this corpus the Vitamin D category is defined as misinformation; (c) the question was asked after the interviewer described the content-analysis findings, so it is a cued recall. 20/46 = 43.5%; the paper prints 43% here and 43.5% elsewhere for the same fraction.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) No overall misinformation share is reported. Table 1's eight categories are Vitamin D 73, tanning as medical treatment 31, indoor tanning equivalent to sunshine 31, safer than outdoor tanning 3, health benefits of tanning 7, skin appearance 40, cancer 7, base tan 29 (of N=4,956 posts). Only the three that carry a printed percentage were extracted; the other five are verbatim counts over the same denominator and could be added (e.g. 40/4956 = 0.8% for skin appearance). Their sum must NOT be taken as a total because coding is not mutually exclusive and R8 forbids cross-category sums. (2) Not extracted: the Discussion summary 'an overall low frequency of social media posts promoting health misinformation (range 0.5%-1.5%)' - a range across categories, not an overall share; recorded here rather than as a range_not_point row. (3) Not extracted: 25/46 (54%) believed it is safe to get Vitamin D from indoor tanning - belief, excluded by protocol; note the paper writes 'Among those participants, approximately half (25/46, 54%)' although 25/46 is over the full sample, not over the 20 who saw the posts, which looks like an editing error. (4) Not extracted: 45/46 (97.8%) used Facebook; 20/46 (43.5%) followed a tanning business - platform use, not misinformation. (5) Not extracted: 4/46 (8.7%) said the posts led them to see tanning as safer than the sun, and the Table 3 influence items - perceived influence/attitudes, not exposure shares. (6) Business-level concentration is described but not quantified as a share (e.g. 3 businesses had 5+ Vitamin D posts, 1 business had 13 base-tan posts), so it fails R1 and no CONCENTRATION row is possible.

rob.design: Two components. (a) Retrospective content analysis of Facebook, 1 May 2015 - 30 Apr 2016: purposeful sampling of 3 indoor tanning business pages per US state (the 3 most-followed among the first 10 search results for 'tanning salon' + [state]) meeting inclusion criteria (official page, UV-tanning focus on 2 of 3 criteria, page >= 1 year old, active in 2015), excluding multi-state chains; 147 pages, of which 3 businesses closed before coding; posts sampled as the final post of every third day of each month, duplicates skipped, yielding 4,956 posts, each post the unit of analysis. Codebook developed from prior codebooks, literature and pilot coding; interrater agreement 84%-99% initially and 91%-100% at end. (b) Qualitative interviews, 8 May - 7 Jul 2017: 46 White non-Hispanic women aged 16-23 who had tanned indoors in the past year, recruited via targeted Facebook advertisements, phone-screened and consented, 20-40 minute phone interviews, US $40 incentive; constant comparative analysis by three investigators with blinded double coding of subsets. IRB: Seattle Children's (15506 exempt; 15710). Authors state external validity was not a goal for the interview sample and note Facebook-only, no Instagram/Snapchat, and 2015-16 data.
rob.item6_quote: The spread of misinformation through social media can be particularly influential, as it is tied to emotions, identity, and one’s social network. For this study we define misinformation as inaccurate or false information.
rob.item10_quote: Of a total of 147 indoor tanning business Facebook pages that were evaluated across 50 states, 3 businesses closed prior to coding initiation. This sample of indoor tanning business Facebook pages yielded 4956 posts. Among 8 health misinformation topics identified, the most common were posts promoting misinformation about Vitamin D (n=73, 1.3%).
